constraints: The appliance cannot use an instance profile, task role, or external federation.
The appliance needs only read-only access to one monitoring service.
The team can establish an access-key rotation and revocation process.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The design carries rotation and migration overhead; when the appliance gains role support, the long-lived user should be removed.
details.errorCorrection: The exception is the credential type, not permission to use administrator or root authority.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM users have long-term credentials, while roles provide temporary credentials. AWS recommends roles whenever the workload supports them, but a role-incompatible legacy integration can require a tightly scoped user as an interim boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: The appliance cannot assume a role, so a service-specific IAM user with minimal read-only permissions and rotation is the least broad supported path.

messages.text: Inability to assume a role does not justify administrator permissions; the user should be scoped to the appliance's actual read-only need.
Root keys are unrestricted and are not an acceptable workload identity.
An ARN alone does not provide credentials or cause a non-AWS appliance to assume a role.

feedback.reason: An IAM user is a constrained exception only when the workload cannot use roles; its permissions and key lifecycle must be managed explicitly.

options.text: Create a narrowly scoped IAM user for the appliance, rotate its access key, and replace the integration when role credentials become possible.
Create an administrator IAM user because long-lived credentials are acceptable for appliances.
Use the account root access key because the appliance needs reliable access.
Embed an IAM role ARN in the appliance without providing a mechanism to obtain temporary credentials.

prompt: A legacy monitoring appliance cannot assume an IAM role and requires an access key. Which design is the narrowest supported exception?

constraints: The identities are IAM users in one account.
The users need the same permission set.
The team wants membership changes to control which users receive the shared policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For workforce access across many accounts, IAM Identity Center permission sets may be a better federation boundary; this question is explicitly about IAM users in one account.
details.errorCorrection: The goal is shared user authorization, not duplicated administrator policies or a workload-role trust path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM groups are collections of IAM users used to assign policies to multiple users. A group is not a principal that can sign in or be nested, but it is a useful management boundary for shared user permissions.
details.scenarioApplication: The 40 users need the same read-only access, so one group policy avoids drift and lets onboarding or offboarding change membership.

messages.text: Duplicating policies increases drift and does not provide a central membership control.
The account root user is not a group-based permission source for IAM users.
Roles are assumed identities with trust policies, not a shared IAM-user membership construct.

feedback.reason: An IAM group provides a shared policy assignment for IAM users and makes membership the central control for the common permission set.

options.text: Place the users in an IAM group and attach the read-only policy to the group.
Copy an administrator policy directly to every user and edit 40 policies for changes.
Attach the policy to the account root user so all users inherit it.
Create 40 roles with identical trust policies and never manage membership.

prompt: A team needs to grant the same read-only S3 permissions to 40 IAM users and update the permissions centrally. Which IAM construct best expresses that shared assignment?

constraints: The instance profile references the intended role.
The role permissions policy already allows the required object read.
The failure occurs before the application can obtain role credentials.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The trust principal should be as narrow as the architecture permits; trusting a whole account or broad service path can enlarge the assumption surface.
details.errorCorrection: Trust and permissions are separate decisions. A role that permits S3 but cannot be assumed is still unusable.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM roles have a trust policy and a permissions policy. The trust policy establishes who or what may assume the role; the permissions policy grants actions after credentials are issued.
details.scenarioApplication: The application cannot obtain credentials because EC2 is not trusted, so changing the trust policy is the required fix; changing S3 permissions cannot repair role assumption.

messages.text: The permissions policy is evaluated after role assumption and cannot make EC2 a trusted principal.
A bucket policy can authorize the role session or role principal after authentication, but it cannot repair the role's trust relationship with EC2.
Root credentials are unrelated to the role trust failure and would create an unsafe workload secret.

feedback.reason: A role must trust the service or principal that assumes it, while the role permissions policy controls what the resulting session can do.

options.text: Update the role trust policy to trust the EC2 service principal, then keep the S3 permission in the role permissions policy.
Add more S3 actions to the role permissions policy because trust policies grant service permissions.
Add the role ARN to the S3 bucket policy and leave the trust policy unchanged.
Create a root access key and place it in the instance user data.

prompt: An EC2 instance has a role whose permissions policy allows `s3:GetObject`, but the instance profile cannot obtain credentials because the role trust policy does not trust EC2. What is the decisive fix?

constraints: The instance profile and trust policy are functioning.
The request uses the intended table ARN and region.
The only missing evidence is the role's permissions policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The policy should be narrowed to the table and required action instead of attaching an account-wide administrator policy to make the error disappear.
details.errorCorrection: Adding a service principal to a trust policy does not grant application data access, and IAM groups are for users rather than roles.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The role trust policy controls assumption; the role permissions policy controls the actions available to the resulting session. The two policies solve different stages of the request.
details.scenarioApplication: Because assumption succeeds and the request is otherwise well-formed, the missing or mismatched DynamoDB allow is the first authorization surface to inspect.

messages.text: Trust policies and S3 bucket policies are not interchangeable, and the question concerns DynamoDB authorization.
The EC2 service principal belongs in role assumption, not as a substitute for an action/resource permission.
IAM roles can receive identity-based permissions policies directly; groups do not attach to roles.

feedback.reason: Once the role is assumed, its permissions policy must allow the requested DynamoDB action on the requested table.

options.text: Verify that the role permissions policy allows `dynamodb:GetItem` on the exact table resource.
Replace the trust policy with a bucket policy because DynamoDB requires S3-style authorization.
Add the EC2 service principal to the table name because trust is controlled by resource names.
Attach an IAM group to the role because roles cannot receive permissions policies.

prompt: An EC2 instance successfully assumes its role, but the application receives `AccessDenied` for `dynamodb:GetItem`. The role trust policy trusts EC2, and no resource policy or explicit deny exists. Where should the architect look first?

constraints: The bucket policy principal, action, and object resource match exactly.
The request is same-account.
No SCP, session policy, ACL, boundary, or explicit deny changes the stated policies.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A cross-account request uses a different evaluation boundary and generally requires authorization in both accounts, so the account relationship must never be left implicit.
details.errorCorrection: The two-sided allow requirement is a cross-account concern; it is not the same-account rule described here.
details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS policy evaluation combines applicable same-account identity-based and resource-based allows, while an explicit deny overrides the result. The exact principal and resource match are decisive.
details.scenarioApplication: The bucket policy directly names the IAM user and allows the exact object read, so the missing identity-policy allow does not prevent the same-account request.

messages.text: A same-account resource-based allow can authorize the request without a matching identity-policy allow when no limiting policy applies.
S3 bucket policies can name IAM user ARNs as principals.
An SCP is a maximum-permissions guardrail, not a required grant for the stated same-account resource-policy allow.

feedback.reason: For the stated same-account case, an applicable resource-based allow can provide the permission when no explicit deny or limiting boundary applies.

options.text: The read is allowed because the applicable same-account resource-policy allow can combine with the identity policy set.
The read is denied because every same-account request requires an identity-policy allow.
The read is denied because S3 bucket policies cannot name an IAM user ARN.
The read is allowed only if an SCP explicitly grants the action.

prompt: An IAM user and an S3 bucket are in the same account. The user has no identity-policy allow for `s3:GetObject`, but the bucket policy allows the user's ARN to read the requested object. No explicit deny or boundary applies. What is the result?

constraints: Both policy statements match the requested principal, action, and object.
The request is authenticated and reaches S3.
No policy condition changes the match.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The fix is to remove or narrow the unintended deny after confirming the security intent; adding more allows cannot override it.
details.errorCorrection: Direct attachment to a role does not make an allow immune to an explicit deny in another applicable policy.
details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS policy evaluation treats an explicit deny in an applicable policy as decisive, regardless of whether an identity policy or resource policy also allows the action.
details.scenarioApplication: The bucket-policy deny matches the same role, action, and object, so the request fails before the two allows could produce access.

messages.text: Role attachment does not override an explicit deny.
Resource policies can explicitly deny role requests when the statement matches.
The stated bucket-policy deny is already sufficient; an SCP is not required for the request to fail.

feedback.reason: An applicable explicit deny takes precedence over all matching allows.

options.text: The request is denied because an applicable explicit deny overrides an allow.
The request succeeds because the identity policy is attached directly to the role.
The request succeeds because resource policies cannot deny role requests.
The request is denied only if an SCP also denies the action.

prompt: An IAM role has an identity policy allowing `s3:GetObject`, but a matching bucket policy explicitly denies the same action for the role. Which effective result should the application expect?

constraints: The identity-policy allow matches the EC2 action.
The boundary is the only limiting boundary and does not allow EC2.
No resource policy, SCP, session policy, or other deny changes the result.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Boundaries are useful delegation guardrails, but they must be analyzed separately from SCPs, resource policies, and explicit denies.
details.errorCorrection: The boundary applies to read and write actions and applies to IAM users as well as roles.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An identity policy can grant an action only within the set allowed by the attached permissions boundary. The boundary does not grant permissions by itself, but it can prevent an identity-policy allow from becoming effective.
details.scenarioApplication: The identity policy allows EC2 while the boundary allows only S3, so the EC2 request is denied.

messages.text: The boundary caps the identity-policy allow and therefore can prevent the call.
Boundaries are not limited to mutating actions; the stated read-only EC2 action is also outside the boundary.
Permissions boundaries can apply to IAM users and IAM roles.

feedback.reason: A permissions boundary sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can receive, so the EC2 action is outside the effective intersection.

options.text: The call is denied because the effective permission must be allowed by both the identity policy and the permissions boundary.
The call succeeds because an identity-policy allow always overrides a boundary.
The call succeeds because boundaries restrict only write actions.
The call is denied because boundaries can be attached only to roles.

prompt: An IAM user has an identity policy allowing `ec2:DescribeInstances`. A permissions boundary attached to that user allows only `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`. There is no explicit deny. What is the result of the EC2 call?

constraints: The role and bucket are in the member account's policy scope.
The identity and resource allows match the delete request.
The SCP's allowed action set is exactly the one stated.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The management-account relationship and member-account scope must be explicit; SCP behavior is not the same as an IAM identity or resource policy.
details.errorCorrection: A resource-based allow does not bypass an applicable Organizations maximum, and an omitted action can be outside an allow-list SCP without an explicit deny.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Effective permissions in a member account require the requested action to be permitted by the applicable SCP as well as by the policies that grant access. SCPs are guardrails, not grants.
details.scenarioApplication: The SCP omits `s3:DeleteObject`, so the role cannot delete even though identity and resource policies allow it.

messages.text: A resource policy cannot bypass an applicable SCP for a member-account principal.
SCPs can constrain individual actions as well as services.
The SCP alone limits the member-account role; a permissions boundary is not required for the denial.

feedback.reason: An SCP limits the maximum permissions available to principals in a member account; it does not grant the omitted delete action.

options.text: The delete is denied because the SCP does not include it in the member account's maximum permissions.
The delete succeeds because the resource policy bypasses the SCP.
The delete succeeds because SCPs can restrict services but not individual actions.
The delete is denied only if a permissions boundary is also attached to the role.

prompt: A role in an Organizations member account has identity and resource policies that allow `s3:DeleteObject`. The applicable SCP allows only `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket`, with no explicit deny. What is the effective result for the delete?

constraints: The caller is authenticated as the trusted role in Account A.
The target role trust policy names that role ARN exactly.
No SCP, boundary, or explicit deny changes the result.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Trusting a specific role ARN is narrower than trusting an entire account or broad principal, but the caller permission must still be explicit.
details.errorCorrection: The target role's permissions policy controls actions after assumption; it does not authorize the initial AssumeRole call.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The caller-side identity policy and target-side trust policy form two distinct sides of a cross-account AssumeRole request. A correct trust policy cannot grant the caller permission to invoke STS.
details.scenarioApplication: The target already trusts the exact caller, so adding `sts:AssumeRole` on the caller for the target role is the missing side.

messages.text: The target role permissions apply after assumption and do not grant the caller `sts:AssumeRole`.
Cross-account role trust can name specific role ARNs; broadening trust would weaken security rather than fix the missing caller permission.
The caller-side permission is required before the target role can be assumed.

feedback.reason: Cross-account role assumption requires the caller to be allowed to assume the role and the target role to trust the caller.

options.text: Grant the caller permission to perform `sts:AssumeRole` on the target role, while retaining the target trust policy.
Add the target role's permissions policy to Account A because trust policies grant caller permissions.
Make the target role trust the entire internet because cross-account access cannot use role ARNs.
Grant the target role access to Account A's resources; the caller's permission is irrelevant.

prompt: A role in Account B trusts a specific role in Account A, but the calling role in Account A has no `sts:AssumeRole` permission. The trust relationship is otherwise correct. What must change?

constraints: The request matches the action and resource in the policy.
The request context does not contain a true MFA-present value.
No other policy grants the action or explicitly denies it.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A policy can use conditions as a least-privilege guardrail, but the identity path must actually provide the context key and value the policy expects.
details.errorCorrection: The presence of an Allow keyword is not sufficient; conditions are part of whether the statement matches.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM evaluates policy conditions against request context keys. A statement whose condition evaluates false does not grant the action, so the request can be implicitly denied without an explicit deny.
details.scenarioApplication: The user did not authenticate with MFA, so `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is not true and the conditional statement does not apply.

messages.text: An Allow with a false condition does not apply to the request.
IAM conditions can govern console and API authorization when the relevant request context is evaluated.
A permissions boundary is not required to explain a conditional allow that does not match.

feedback.reason: A conditional allow grants access only when its condition matches; without MFA in the request context, no applicable allow remains.

options.text: The conditional allow does not match the request context, so the action remains implicitly denied.
The action must succeed because the policy contains an Allow statement.
The condition is ignored for console requests because MFA applies only to API calls.
The user needs a permissions boundary that denies S3 before the condition can be evaluated.

prompt: An IAM policy allows `s3:GetObject` only when `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is true. A user signs in to the console with a password but without MFA and receives `AccessDenied`. What explains the result?

constraints: The application uses STS role-assumption credentials.
The bucket policy is intended to constrain the assumed session.
The role permissions policy and the resource policy may be evaluated through different principal representations.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Precise principal scoping improves least privilege but increases the need for explicit policy evaluation and testing when sessions are used.
details.errorCorrection: STS sessions are the normal temporary credential path and can access services when the effective policy set allows them.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A role session has a session principal and temporary credentials. Resource-policy behavior can depend on whether a policy names the role principal or the session principal and on which policy types and conditions apply.
details.scenarioApplication: The application uses an assumed session, so the first diagnostic step is to verify the effective principal representation rather than assume every role ARN reference behaves identically.

messages.text: Role and session principal behavior is not interchangeable in every policy context; the exact resource-policy semantics matter.
Replacing a temporary session with root credentials would worsen the security posture and is not a diagnostic fix.
Resource-based policies can participate in authorization for assumed-role requests; removing them can break intended access.

feedback.reason: Authorization diagnostics must distinguish the IAM role from the assumed role session and inspect the exact principal and conditions that apply to the request.

options.text: Verify the exact role or role-session principal and all applicable policy context used by the request.
Assume that the role ARN and every role-session ARN are interchangeable in every resource policy condition.
Replace the role with a root access key because STS sessions cannot access S3.
Remove all resource policies because assumed roles use only identity policies.

prompt: An S3 bucket policy grants access to the IAM role ARN, but an application assumes that role and the request is evaluated as a role session. No explicit deny exists. What should the architect verify first when diagnosing an unexpected authorization result?

constraints: The users are IAM users and need a self-service credential path.
The application-data actions can be separated from credential-management actions.
The organization wants MFA to be a condition for the data actions.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The organization must verify how its sign-in path supplies MFA context and should prefer federated temporary credentials for workforce access where available.
details.errorCorrection: Root MFA protects the root account and does not automatically require MFA for IAM users; user data access needs its own applicable policy condition.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM policies can use conditions such as MFA context on selected statements. Separating permissions keeps the credential-management path usable while making the application-data path conditional.
details.scenarioApplication: The user needs both capabilities, but only the data actions require MFA, so the two policy concerns should not be collapsed into one broad allow.

messages.text: Root MFA does not enforce MFA for IAM-user data actions.
AdministratorAccess ignores the least-privilege and MFA-conditioned requirement.
A permissions boundary is a maximum-permissions guardrail and does not evaluate a typed MFA code as an interactive policy input.

feedback.reason: Separating self-service credential permissions from application permissions lets the policy require MFA specifically for the sensitive data actions.

options.text: Allow the required credential-management actions separately and condition the application-data allow on MFA presence.
Require MFA only for the root user and leave the IAM users' data actions unconditional.
Put every permission in one unconditional AdministratorAccess policy and rely on user training.
Use a permissions boundary that grants data access only when a user types an MFA code into the policy.

prompt: A company wants IAM users to manage their own credentials but not to access application data unless they authenticate with MFA. Which policy design best expresses the requirement?
